* Environmental Kuznets curve literature documents nonlinear income–emissions relationships.
- Grossman-Pauketat-Keiley (1995) report inverted-U patterns; Selden-Park (1999) question robustness across datasets.
* Empirical macro studies test bidirectional income-growth–CO2-emission causality.
- Pedronce panel cointegration detects long-run associations; Granger tests reveal mixed short-run feedback across country groups.
* Structural-break analyses challenge stable EKC estimates.
- Bai-Perron break tests expose regime-dependent emissions responses; policy-shock years alter carbon-income elasticities.
* Trade-openness dynamics mediate growth–emission pathways.
- Frankel-Rosado (2005) find trade liberalization potentially raises emissions; energy-intensity controls mitigate spurious growth correlations.
* Financial development studies identify ambiguous emission effects.
- Ionescu-Petrescu (2021) document financial-deepening–lower-carbon-intensity associations; green-sector credit allocation matters.
* Renewable-energy adoption research connects decarbonization–inclusive growth.
- Apergis-Tarazi (2012) evidence renewable-energy–emission decoupling; policy-support mechanisms sustain growth avoiding fossil-fuel dependency.
* Methodological advances stress identification, heterogeneity, robustness.
- DID, synthetic-control, threshold-panel models reduce endogeneity; country-group results diverge sharply.
* Policy implications converge: low-carbon innovation, pricing instruments, structural transformation.
- Carbon-pricing simulations show modest welfare costs; technology diffusion accelerates emission intensity declines.
